stem: A 64-year-old patient was given antibiotics to fight off a post-operative neck infection. Two days later, he presents to the clinic in a worse condition and a CT shows evidence of infection in the mediastinum. How did the infection travel to his mediastinum?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

There are no actual spaces in the body, only potential spaces. One potential space is between the two fascial planes, the pretracheal fascia and the prevertebral fascia, called the retropharyngeal space. This space communicates directly to the mediastinum. Thus, if an infection gets into the retropharyngeal space it may be able to spread to the mediastinum.

stem: At a recent visit to the emergency room yesterday, Nellie discovered that her previous 2- week history of palpitations were due to atrial fibrillation. She was prescribed anticoagulation therapy to reduce the risk of thrombosis/embolism. Today, she developed numbness and paralysis in her tongue and pallor in her face, consistent with embolism. Mentation is normal and there are no other symptoms. Based on this presentation, occlusion has likely occurred in an artery that branched off the _____.
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The vertebral artery runs along the spinal cord straight to the brain with minimal branching. The common carotid artery bifurcates into the internal carotid artery and the external carotid artery, and the external carotid artery has many branches which supply blood to the face - including the tongue (lingual artery).

stem: An 80-year-old presents to your clinic with a lateral neck mass. She describes the neck mass as being present for the past 3 months. Before you begin your physical examination, what is the most likely diagnosis for this patient’s presentation?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

About 80% of lateral head and neck masses are neoplastic (and 80% of neoplasms are malignant). In addition, neoplasms become a more common diagnosis in the elderly. A lymphatic malformation is a congenital defect that is commonly associated with a longer timeline (>7 years) and is usually noticeable shortly after birth. A thyroid goiter would present as a more medial neck mass. Suppurative Lymphadenitis occurs when a lymph node becomes infected and this usually resolves within a few weeks.

Perform an ultrasound and request a CT scan
Perform an incisional biopsy for pathologic analysis
Incision and drainage for the cyst for analysis of its components

A family doctor should attempt imaging of a neck mass prior to referring to an ENT doctor. For neck and head masses, common imaging modalities are ultrasound and CT scans. While a biopsy may be ordered, imaging is likely to be ordered first, and also, a less invasive FNA biopsy is a better choice than an incisional biopsy. Lastly, the presentation (firm, irregular, fixed) does not indicate a cyst.

stem: Which of the following larynx pathologies most likely involves airway stabilization as an immediate management step?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Bilateral vocal cord paralysis can obstruct the flow air into and out of the lungs, thus an immediate consideration is always airways stabilization. With unilateral vocal cord paralysis airway management is not an immediate concern, and a long-term approach may be taken involving voice therapy and watchful waiting. Laryngopharyngeal reflux and vocal fold nodules are fairly common and do not require airway management as an immediate consideration.

stem: Which option correctly describes a cause and a treatment of the associated laryngeal pathology?

options.html: Laryngeal nodules are caused by voice overuse and are treated surgically
Laryngeal polyps are caused by laryngeal trauma and treated with voice rest
Laryngopharyngeal reflux is caused by stomach acid reflux and is treated with PPIs
Early vocal cord cancer is treated with complete laryngectomy

answer:
The correct answer is C.

In laryngopharyngeal reflux, excess stomach acid from the esophagus enters the larynx causing hoarseness. PPIs (proton-pump inhibitors) decrease the acidity of the gastric juices. Laryngeal nodules are treated with voice rest, laryngeal polyps are treated surgically, and early vocal cord cancer is treated with endoscopic laser. Advanced vocal cord cancer is treated with complete laryngectomy.

stem: A patient presented to an urgent care clinic after an episode of choking during dinner. He thinks he may have accidentally inhaled part of a chicken wing. His vitals are currently stable, but physical examination reveals stridor when inhaling only. Based on the physical examination, the chicken wing was most likely lodged in which part of the patient’s airway?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Stridor can be inspiratory, expiratory (wheeze) or bi-phasic. Inspiratory stridor is usually caused by an obstruction of the supraglottis or glottis. Biphasic stridor is usually caused by an obstruction of the subglottis. Expiratory wheeze is usually caused by an obstruction in the lower lungs (and based on anatomy, obstruction of the right bronchus is most common). The piriform sinuses are not part of the airway and would not result in stridor or wheeze.

stem: Several months ago, Troy (6 years old) had a laryngitis with severe airflow restriction. Lately, his teacher noticed that Troy is significantly more fatigued in gym class and uncharacteristically becomes exhausted quickly after exertion. Today on physical examination, Troy demonstrates both stridor and wheeze. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely?

options.html: Foreign body aspiration lodged in the supraglottic area

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Presence of biphasic stridor (inspiratory and expiratory) indicates an obstruction of the subglottis. Subglottic stenosis could be congenital, but is often iatrogenic after a previous intubation – this is consistent with Troy’s past medical history. Subglottic hemangioma is a congenital obstruction and would likely have presented in gym class prior to Troy’s intubation. Croup would cause a characteristic “barking cough”, and a foreign body in the supraglottic area would likely cause inspiratory stridor only.

options.html: Consider measuring the patients INR and PTT
Counsel the patient to pinch their nose where cartilage meets bone
Obtain the patient’s blood type to prepare for transfusion

answer:
The correct answer is C.

This patient has lost a lot of blood and may need transfusions - her blood type should be obtained. The patient is on warfarin (an anticoagulant with a narrow therapeutic window), so iatrogenic causes of bleeding should be ruled in or out with INR/PTT tests. Vitamin K is a reversing agent of warfarin and may be needed if these are elevated. Tranexamic acid is a hemostatic agent to slow blood loss. With nosebleeds, patients should be counseled to pinch their nostrils shut for 10-15 minutes - pinching the bridge of the nose where bone meets cartilage is “common knowledge” but also incorrect

stem: What is the best treatment for a patient who complains of odynophagia and referred otalgia, and whose physical exam demonstrates uvular deviation and unilateral peritonsillar swelling? The pain and swelling have been progressing for the past week.

options.html: This is likely a viral infection – watch and wait
This is likely a gram + infection – treat with penicillin

This is likely a tumor – surgical removal with adjuvant radiation therapy
This is likely sialolithiasis (salivary gland stones) – hydrate and manage the gland
This is likely acute sinusitis – endoscopic sinus surgery and IV antibiotics

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The rapid onset implies an infection, and the referred otalgia indicates a pathology in the oropharynx. This patient’s presentation is consistent with peritonsillar abscess (uni-lateral, uvular deviation, and location in the oropharynx). Abscesses are treated with incision and drainage. Note - If this were tonsillitis, a culture would need to be obtained to identify the pathogen and prescribe a treatment.

options.html: Originate from other organs and metastasize to the neck
Are derived from cells of epithelial origin
Are derived from the salivary glands
All of the above are true
None of the above are true

answer: B) Metastases to the neck are rare, malignancies of the head and neck are typically primary tumors. Most of these malignancies are derived from the lining of the upper aerodigestive tract (NOT the skin, thyroid, salivary glands etc..). Most head and neck tumors are of epithelial origin (i.e. squamous cell carcinoma of the upper aerodigestive tract), and not mesenchymal origin (sarcomas).

stem: Your patient presents with a sore throat and fever for the past three days. Upon examination, you notice an enlarged pus-filled tonsil on the right side, causing the uvula to deviate to the left. What is your most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

A peritonsillar abscess would cause similar symptoms to tonsillitis, but a deviating uvula and pus-filled tonsil is more suggestive of a peritonsillar abscess.

stem: If the hypoglossal (CN XII) nerve is injured, which direction will the tongue deviate towards?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

When the hypoglossal nerve is injured, the tongue will deviate towards the affected side.
